## Introduction

For this project, I continued observational data collection that began in Project 2, focusing on **café beverage orders** as my subject of observation. Specifically, I recorded details about drinks being purchased at a local café, noting the type of drink, its size, its price in NZD, and the time of day the order was placed. Each observation was logged via a Google Form immediately after witnessing a drink order, ensuring accuracy and consistency.

The purpose of this data collection was to explore patterns in everyday café consumption behaviour — a topic that is both personally relevant and statistically interesting. I was curious whether certain drink types are systematically more expensive, whether there are predictable peak times for café orders, and whether drink size reliably predicts the price paid.

No new questions were added to the Google Form from Project 2, as the existing five variables — `Timestamp`, `drink_type`, `size`, `price_nzd`, and `time_of_day` — were sufficient to address the three analytical questions I wanted to explore in this project.

Data collection for this project was carried out by myself only. I collected a total of **25 observations** across multiple days in March and April 2026. Observations were made during both morning and afternoon café visits, providing coverage across different times of day.

The process of creating visualisations required careful thought about which variables to pair together and which chart types would communicate the relationships most clearly. For the first visualisation, I chose a horizontal bar chart (`geom_col`) to compare average prices across drink types, because bar charts are ideal for comparing a numerical summary across discrete categories. For the second, I used an area-and-line chart (`geom_area` + `geom_line`) to show how observation frequency changed across hours of the day, because this geom effectively highlights the volume and shape of temporal patterns. For the third, I used a boxplot (`geom_boxplot`) with jittered individual points overlaid, as this combination shows both the summary distribution and the raw data simultaneously — making outliers visible and the spread of prices interpretable.

I initially experimented with a violin plot for the size-price comparison, but found that with only 25 observations the violin shapes were not meaningful. Switching to a boxplot with jitter provided a cleaner and more honest representation of the data at this sample size. All three visualisations use a warm coffee-toned colour palette to maintain visual consistency with the HTML data story.

## Visual data story

My visual data story is published and accessible at the following URL:

[https://yourusername.github.io/stats220/visual_data_story.html](https://yourusername.github.io/stats220/visual_data_story.html)

*(Replace `yourusername` with your actual GitHub username before submitting.)*

The visual data story demonstrates creativity in several ways. First, the overall design uses a custom CSS colour theme inspired by the subject matter — warm coffee browns and creams — which creates a cohesive aesthetic that goes beyond the default R Markdown styling. Second, the story is structured as a genuine narrative with three progressively revealed sections, each posing a question before answering it with a visualisation. This question-and-answer structure guides the reader through the data in a logical, engaging way rather than simply presenting figures one after another. Third, JavaScript-based progressive reveal on scroll was included to create a smooth, modern reading experience that standard R Markdown output does not provide by default. Fourth, the caption and highlight-box CSS elements were custom-designed to draw attention to key data source information and to visually separate different components of each section, improving both readability and accessibility.

## Learning reflection

The most important idea I learned from Module 4 — Creating Visual-Based Communications — is the concept of the **grammar of graphics** as implemented in `{ggplot2}`. Before this module, I thought of charts as fixed templates (bar chart, pie chart, line chart). Learning that every visualisation is built from composable layers — data, aesthetic mappings, geometric objects, scales, and themes — fundamentally changed how I approach data visualisation. It means that instead of choosing a chart type and fitting data into it, I now think about *what relationship I want to show* first, and then build the layers needed to show it clearly. This was directly useful in Project 4, where I had to decide why a boxplot with jitter was a better choice than a violin plot for a small dataset.

Going forward, I am most curious about **interactive visualisations** using packages like `{plotly}` or `{ggiraph}`, which can convert static `{ggplot2}` outputs into interactive charts with hover tooltips, zooming, and filtering. I am also curious about `{shiny}`, which would allow a viewer to select which drink type or time period to display — turning a static story into a dynamic, user-driven exploration. These tools seem like the natural next step after mastering static visualisation, and I can see them being valuable in both academic and professional data communication contexts.
